items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: 13,544 weekly downloads, up 11.5% in a day and 200% since 4 August, while stars moved 0.5%. Seventh straight appearance, and the gap between installing it and bookmarking it has never once closed.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: TheRealYT/git-knife
items.brief: 291 stars, up 12.3%, with 165 HackerNews points and 101 comments. Open issues up 33.3% on the same day: the people who found it are using it hard enough to file bugs.
items.description: A desktop GUI for editing git commit metadata: the message, the author, and both the author and the committer dates. Existing git interfaces reword and reorder commits well but treat dates as fixed, and the tools that can rewrite them, git-filter-repo and commit-tree, have no interface at all. git-knife covers that gap by shelling out to the system git and rebuilding each commit from its original tree, so file contents are provably never altered.

items.name: antigma.ai
items.brief: Forks up 30.8% against stars up 12.7% in a day, 50 forks on 1,652 stars. Pushed the same day, and HackerNews has gone quiet at 1.8%, so the growth is running without a thread behind it.
items.description: Antigma, a terminal harness for running AI coding agents, published as the repository AntigmaLabs/ante. The agent loop, the tool calls and the sandbox ship in a single binary rather than being assembled from separate services, so the whole run happens on one machine and can be inspected afterwards. For a tool of this kind the fork count is the number that carries information: forking means taking the code away to change it, which is a different act from starring it.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Weekly downloads 11,161, up 7% today and up 147% since the 4,518 recorded nine days ago. Stars moved 0% and forks 1.1% in the same window. Six appearances and the gap has widened on every one of them — attention flat, installation compounding. Ordinarily downloads follow stars; here they have decoupled entirely, and that decoupling is the single most useful pattern this list has produced so far.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. items.name: AntigmaLabs/ante
items.brief: Stars up 14.1% and forks up 10.2% while HackerNews went the other way — front page presence gone entirely, posts down 33%, comments up 1.1%. The thread ended and the growth did not, which is the transition worth watching for and the second repo this month to show it. 34 forks on 1,443 stars is a modest 2.4% ratio, so the people arriving are mostly still evaluating rather than building on it.
items.description: Ante, a self contained harness for running AI coding agents in a terminal, published by Antigma Labs and also reachable at antigma.ai. It does the job of Claude Code or Codex without their dependencies or model constraints, shipping as a single prebuilt binary that is straightforward to drop into a container. The project is explicit that it is an alpha preview and that the core is not yet open source.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Weekly downloads 9,386, up 11.2% today and more than doubled since the 4,518 recorded four days ago. Stars moved 1.6% in the same window — downloads are now growing seven times faster than attention, which is the inversion this list exists to catch. Fifth appearance and the gap has widened each time. Whatever is happening here is happening in package managers, not on forums.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: antirez/h3.c
items.brief: Stars up 117%, forks up 96%, open issues up 183% and HackerNews comments up 453% in a single day. 71 forks on 1,432 stars is a 5% ratio within hours, and 13 open issues means people are running it on their own machines rather than reading the README.
items.description: An inference engine written in C that runs the MiniMax H3 language model on Apple hardware, from Salvatore Sanfilippo, who wrote Redis. Its claim is that a model this size can be served from one self contained C program with no Python runtime and no framework at all. That matters because the usual stack is several gigabytes of dependencies before the model itself is even loaded.

items.name: palamim/starboard
items.brief: Second appearance, and stars, forks and open issues all moved together again at 3.1%, 3.6% and 20%. Pushed today rather than abandoned after the thread. At this size that is a handful of people, and it is the same handful coming back.
items.description: A macOS terminal that sits permanently beside the Dock instead of appearing on a hotkey. It stays on screen across every Space, including over full screen apps, and never takes focus from whatever you are working in. Inside it is a real login shell, so directory, history and state carry between commands rather than each one starting fresh. The bet is that a terminal you glance at gets used differently from one you summon.

items.name: palamim/starboard
items.brief: Stars up 4.9%, forks up 6.7%, open issues up 20% — modest across the board and consistent in direction, which on a 144-star repo means a handful of real users rather than a crowd. A terminal pinned beside the Dock is a narrow idea with an obvious audience, and the fork-to-star ratio suggests some of them are already changing it. Two days since the last push.
items.description: A macOS terminal that sits permanently beside the Dock instead of appearing on a hotkey. It stays on screen across every Space, including over full screen apps, and never takes focus from whatever you are working in. items.name: MakazhanAlpamys/Soup
items.brief: 68 open issues against 430 stars is a 16% ratio, five times what a young repo usually carries, and forks are up 5.5% against 3% star growth. The people arriving are running it and hitting walls rather than bookmarking it. HackerNews has gone quiet at 0.7%.
items.description: Fine tunes a large language model from a single YAML file, with no SSH into a training box and no framework configuration to assemble. It streams layers rather than loading the whole model, which is what lets an 8 billion parameter model train on a laptop GPU with 4 GB of memory. Distributed on PyPI as soup-cli, so installs are countable separately from stars.

items.name: t8y2/dbx
items.brief: Third appearance. 13,242 stars with 1,344 forks is one fork per ten stars, where most repos manage one in fifty, and the ratio has held for a week rather than spiking and fading. Homebrew installs are the number to watch, because a package manager install puts it on a machine.
items.description: A desktop database client that speaks to more than 70 systems, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, MongoDB, DuckDB and SQL Server among them, in a 20 MB download. The same build ships as a desktop app, a Docker image and a command line tool, with an AI assistant and an MCP server included. Most clients of this scope are hundreds of megabytes, so the size is the claim being made.

items.name: runtimewire.com
items.brief: Pricing tiers up 33.3%, which means it added a plan, and a new plan is the monetisation trigger this system treats as a signal on its own. On the HackerNews front page the same day with 22 comments.
items.description: A news site covering the AI industry as it happens: funding rounds, model launches, infrastructure changes and founder moves, filed as short scoops rather than weekly summaries. It competes on speed of publication against the general technology press, so the interesting measurement for a site like this is whether readers arrive directly or only through aggregators.

items.name: xoreaxeaxeax/asm-hall-of-shame
items.brief: Stars up 38.4% in a day, forks up 12%, open issues up 20%, with GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters all seeing it at once. Lobsters points more than doubled at 108.8%. Five forks on 567 stars this early says people are submitting entries, not just reading them.
items.description: A leaderboard for the slowest possible single machine instruction, from the reverse engineer behind the sandsifter processor fuzzer. Instruction analysis normally chases speed; this deliberately searches for the floor. The current x86 champion takes 198 billion cycles, about 62 seconds, by making one instruction load processor state across a deliberately saturated PCIe fabric. Setup can be anything, but only one instruction is scored.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Weekly downloads up 9.7% while the week-over-week growth figure itself jumped 342% — the acceleration is accelerating, which is the rarer of the two readings. 4,518 downloads a week now against 1,621 stars means more people are installing it than have bothered to bookmark it, and that ratio almost never runs this way round. 82 open issues on a library this young is the healthy kind of noise. Fourth appearance and the first where downloads, not attention, are doing the work.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: V4bel/Zapscape
items.brief: Three independent collectors on day one, GitHub, HackerNews and Lobsters at once. Stars and forks both up 12.9% in exact lockstep, with Lobsters comments up 25%. Ten forks on 110 stars this early says people are running the exploit to see it work.
items.description: A working exploit and write up for CVE-2026-64561, a guest to host escape in KVM on x86. The bug is a use after free in the shadow MMU, in the recursive path that runs when shadow pages are reclaimed, and a guest can trigger it alone to reach the host kernel with root privilege. It is the third in a series from the same researcher, published after the coordinated embargo ended.

items.name: pg83/shitty
items.brief: Fourth day and the shape has held. Open issues up 42.9% against 2% star growth, long after HackerNews stopped talking, where comments moved 1.2%. Most launch driven repos flatten within seventy two hours. This one kept the adoption after losing the audience.
items.description: A terminal emulator built for low latency and fast startup, keeping terminal state on the CPU and rendering cells through Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS. The README publishes head to head throughput against ghostty, alacritty and kitty with every terminal equalised first, which is unusual enough to be worth noting. The same code ships under two names for people who would rather not type the first one.

items.name: pg83/shitty
items.brief: Third appearance, and this is where a thread and a trend separate. Stars up 6.7% and open issues up 16.7%, while HackerNews comments moved 0.6% — the discussion has stopped and the adoption has not. That is the transition most launches never make, and for a terminal emulator with a deliberately absurd name it is more than it had any right to expect.
items.description: A terminal emulator built for low latency and fast startup, keeping terminal state on the CPU and rendering cells through Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS. The same code ships under two names for people who would rather not type the first one.

items.name: veedstudio/open-edit
items.brief: Second day and the ratios held. Stars up 8.2%, forks up 12.1%, with forks again outpacing stars: 141 stars and 8 forks yesterday, 172 and 12 today. At that size a dozen people move it, so the direction carries the information rather than the magnitude.
items.description: An open source video editing pipeline from VEED that has no timeline and no interface. Editing happens entirely through a coding agent: cut and reframe footage, layer motion graphics, turn slides or web pages into video. Source footage is optional, since stills and generated media are enough for some briefs. The renderer is free to use but closed, while everything driving it is open.

items.name: googleworkspace/cli
items.brief: GitHub, Homebrew and npm all seeing it at once, and Homebrew is the one that counts. A package manager entry means somebody installed it deliberately rather than starring it in a browser tab. It carries no fixed command list, building itself from Google's Discovery Service at runtime, so it covers whatever the APIs expose today.
items.description: One command line tool covering Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, Docs, Chat and Admin, published in Google's own GitHub organisation but explicitly not an officially supported Google product. It carries no fixed list of commands. It reads Google's Discovery Service at runtime and builds its command surface from whatever the APIs currently expose, so new endpoints appear without a release. Output is structured JSON, and 40 agent skills ship with it.

items.name: veedstudio/open-edit
items.brief: Stars up 14.7% and forks up 17.9% on the same day, from a base of 141 and 8 — small enough that a handful of people move the percentages, so read the direction rather than the size. What makes it worth a line is the pitch: a video editor you own instead of rent, driven by a coding agent. That is two trends arriving at once, and it is day one on this list.
items.description: An open source video editing pipeline from VEED that has no timeline and no interface. Editing happens entirely through a coding agent: cut and reframe footage, layer motion graphics, turn slides or web pages into video. Source footage is optional, since stills and generated media are enough for some briefs. The renderer is free to use but closed, while everything driving it is open.

items.name: garagehq/nightcrawler
items.brief: Forks jumped 32.7% against 23.3% star growth in a day, and watchers rose 25% — three ratios moving together, which is rarer and harder to fake than any one of them spiking. 44 forks on 593 stars is a 7% ratio on a repo this small, meaning the people finding it are running it rather than filing it. A local AI red-teamer that works on a phone is a specific enough claim to attract either real users or real scepticism, and the 34 comments against 118 HackerNews points suggest more of the first.
items.description: An autonomous penetration testing agent that runs entirely on a phone. Left on a network, it discovers hosts, probes services, tests for known vulnerabilities and writes a report, with no cloud connection anywhere in the loop. A 1.2 billion parameter model running on the phone's GPU decides what to do next. It works slowly and one action at a time, which makes it far harder to spot than a scanner that hits every host at once.

items.name: brian-armstrong/fec
items.brief: A Rust library for forward error correction, on the list with GitHub and HackerNews agreeing. Error-correction code is infrastructure nobody adopts casually — it either solves a problem someone has or it sits unused — so the thing to watch is not stars but whether anyone depends on it. No package downloads yet, which is the number that would turn this from interesting to real.
items.description: A Rust library implementing the two error correcting codes that appear throughout software defined radio and spacecraft links: convolutional codes with a Viterbi decoder, and Reed Solomon codes including the CCSDS standard used on satellite downlinks. With SIMD enabled it decodes faster than libfec, the long standing C implementation, on every code, measured through libfec's own test programs.

items.name: chipsandcheese.com
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 1700% and best rank up 48.5%, on a publication doing deep processor analysis. The percentage is enormous because the base was one comment, so this is a single post landing rather than a trend — the useful question is whether the rank holds next week once the thread is gone, which is exactly what a daily time-series is for.
items.description: A publication that takes apart processor microarchitecture in public, running its own memory bandwidth and latency benchmarks rather than reprinting vendor slides. Recent pieces cover AMD's Instinct accelerators, Arm's efficiency cores and NVIDIA whitepapers. It is one of a small number of outlets doing this depth of hardware analysis outside a chip company.

items.name: 0xchasercat/draco
items.brief: A drop-in replacement for Firecrawl, which is a paid crawling service — so this is the open-source-undercuts-incumbent shape, and those either die quietly or move fast. At 67 stars it is far too early to call, but open issues jumped 50% today against 2.8% star growth, meaning the few people who found it are using it hard enough to break it. Two days since the last push.
items.description: A web scraper written in Rust that returns clean Markdown and metadata from any URL, built as a drop in replacement for Firecrawl and Browserbase. It uses a browser faithful TLS fingerprint to reach pages that block ordinary clients, so a standard page is one fetch and a parse in roughly 300 milliseconds with no headless browser involved. Pages that only render through JavaScript are handled separately.

items.name: pg83/shitty
items.brief: A terminal emulator whose HackerNews thread drew 160 comments against 172 points — a 93% comment-to-point ratio, roughly triple what a well-received post produces. That shape means argument, not applause, and for a terminal emulator the argument is always the same one: whether the world needs another. Stars up 5.7% and forks up 5.4% on the same day says some readers stopped arguing and cloned it.
items.description: A terminal emulator built for low latency and fast startup, keeping terminal state on the CPU and rendering cells through Vulkan on Linux and Metal on macOS. The README publishes head to head throughput against ghostty, alacritty and kitty with every terminal equalised first, which is unusual enough to be worth noting. The same code ships under two names for people who would rather not type the first one.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Stars have more than doubled in five days, 2,196 to 4,945, and forks are still outpacing them — 7.8% against 5.6% in the last day alone. Open issues rose 11.6% in the same window, which on a young repo means people hitting real edges rather than admiring the README. Five days on this list and the ratios have not softened, which is the part that separates a thread from a trend.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model on any Apple Silicon Mac in about 2 GB of memory, including the 8 GB machines, instead of loading all 14.3 GB. It keeps the shared core and the cache resident and streams only the experts each token actually needs off the SSD. The runtime, installer, command line tool and Mac app are all written in Swift and Metal, built for this one model rather than wrapping MLX or llama.cpp.

items.name: t8y2/dbx
items.brief: 1,344 forks and 1,117 open issues against 13,242 stars, which is an extraordinarily engaged ratio — one fork for every ten stars, where most repos manage one in fifty. The signal today is not the star count but Homebrew: it is installable through a package manager, which is the point a tool stops being a repo people star and becomes one they run. Downloads up 2% week over week is modest, and the install path is the thing to watch.
items.description: A desktop database client that speaks to more than 70 systems, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Redis, MongoDB, DuckDB and SQL Server among them, in a 20 MB download. The same build ships as a desktop app, a Docker image and a command line tool, with an AI assistant and an MCP server included. Most clients of this scope are hundreds of megabytes, so the size is the claim being made.

items.name: wie-project/kakehashi
items.brief: A userspace translation layer letting macOS binaries run on Linux ARM64 — technically the hardest kind of project on this list and the kind that usually stalls. 252 HackerNews points against 64 comments is an unusually low argument ratio, which for infrastructure means people are impressed rather than sceptical. 341 stars is small; the engineering claim is what makes it worth watching.
items.description: A translation layer that runs macOS ARM64 binaries on Linux, the reverse of the usual direction. It loads Mach-O executables, maps a standalone libSystem and translates BSD system calls at the boundary, with no JIT and no instruction emulator, because both sides are already the same architecture. Real macOS command line tools then run natively on Linux aarch64.

items.name: pudding.cool
items.brief: The Pudding, a visual-essay publication, with 157 HackerNews comments and its best rank up 23.3%. Comments are actually down 16% from the previous window, so the thread is past its peak; what put this here is the rank move, which follows front-page placement rather than leading it. Attention, not adoption.
items.description: The Pudding, a digital publication that answers cultural questions with interactive visual essays rather than articles. Recent pieces analyse 200,000 similes from popular fiction, track a thousand people through their relationships, and map the vocabulary taught to English learners over time. Each essay is a custom built page, which is why the site is cited as a reference for data journalism.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Forks are growing faster than stars — 10.1% against 8.3% — which is the ratio that separates a tool people run from one they bookmark, and 231 forks on 4,671 stars is high for a repo this young. The HackerNews thread drew 343 comments against 913 points, a 38% ratio meaning argument rather than applause; for a claim about fitting Gemma 4 into 2 GB, the argument is the story. Pushed today, so the maintainer is still in it.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model on any Apple Silicon Mac in about 2 GB of memory, including the 8 GB machines, instead of loading all 14.3 GB. It keeps the shared core and the cache resident and streams only the experts each token actually needs off the SSD. The runtime, installer, command line tool and Mac app are all written in Swift and Metal, built for this one model rather than wrapping MLX or llama.cpp.

items.name: ssp.sh
items.brief: A data-engineering blog whose HackerNews numbers moved 20% on a base of four points. The percentage is real and the base is far too small to carry it — this is here because two unrelated collectors happened to see it, not because anything large happened. Worth a second look only if it returns later in the week.
items.description: A data engineering blog by Simon Späti, published alongside a public notebook of more than a thousand interlinked notes and an online book on data engineering patterns. The deep dives cover the open source data ecosystem, orchestration, modelling and architecture, and the whole thing is navigable as a graph rather than a reverse chronological list.

items.name: Claude Opus 5
items.brief: Third on ProductHunt with 450 votes, and the only launch today carrying independent search demand alongside it. That distinction matters more than the rank: a launch is something that happens to a product, while search interest is people going looking of their own accord, and it is the harder of the two to manufacture. Read the search signal, treat the vote count as the noise around it.
items.description: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5 model, posted to Product Hunt on release day. The listing is a launch record rather than a product page, so what it measures is how a frontier model release lands with an audience that is mostly building software on top of one.

items.name: diataxis.fr
items.brief: Diátaxis is a framework for structuring technical documentation into four modes, and it drew 59 HackerNews comments today. The 0.9% move in its traffic rank arrived alongside that thread rather than before it, so this is attention rather than adoption — the useful question is whether the rank holds next week once the thread is gone. That test is exactly what a daily time-series is for.
items.description: Diátaxis, a framework for organising technical documentation around four separate needs: tutorials for learning, how to guides for a task in hand, reference for looking things up and explanation for understanding. Its argument is that these four fail when mixed, and that documentation should be structured by the reader's situation rather than by the software's feature list. It has been adopted by Django, Cloudflare and Gatsby among others.

items.name: worksinprogress.news
items.brief: A magazine covering underrated ideas in science and policy, with 59 HackerNews comments today. Same shape as the other front-page domains on this list: real discussion, a half-percent nudge to its traffic rank, and no evidence yet that separates a good post from a growing publication.
items.description: Works in Progress, a magazine of underrated ideas in science, technology and public policy, published as long essays with the arguments and the data set out in full. Recent pieces cover the pace of medical progress, the upper limits of animal breeding and why unattractive buildings make housing harder to build. Its readership overlaps heavily with the progress studies and policy world.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Fourth day on the list and the only entry today confirmed by three unrelated collectors — npm downloads, GitHub stars and HackerNews. Downloads are up 41% week over week against 4.4% star growth, and 65 open issues on 1,296 stars is a high ratio: people are running it in anger rather than admiring it. The watcher count sits at 3, which is the one discordant note — almost nobody has committed to following the project despite using it.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: mokshablr/gander
items.brief: 207 HackerNews points and 75 comments against 287 stars and 4 forks. Attention running well ahead of adoption: a lot of people read about it, very few took it home. Stars grew 7.4% and forks 9.1% overnight, so the gap is closing slowly rather than not at all. It has already left the front page, which makes the next two days the test.
items.description: An Android file viewer that opens PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, images, video, audio, Markdown and code in one app, entirely on the device. It is about 8 MB, holds no permissions at all and does not even request internet access, so it cannot send a file anywhere. The gap it fills is that most phones ship several partial viewers that bounce documents to a cloud service to render them.

items.name: wikif1.org
items.brief: An F1 wiki with 1.5% rank movement and 1% subnet growth. Genuinely marginal — it clears the corroboration bar because two independent sources both registered the same small climb. Listed for honesty about what today's threshold admits.
items.description: An independent Formula 1 site carrying race news, driver standings, the season schedule and results, with no affiliation to the sport's official channels. It publishes on race weekends and through the summer break, which is when a season site either keeps its audience or loses it.

items.name: playscrabble.com
items.brief: Same shape as createcentercv: three sources, all agreeing, none dramatic. Rank up 5.4% with subnets up 2%. A long-established word-game site — this is what steady looks like, and it is here to show that the corroboration rule fires on ordinary movement too, not only on spikes.
items.description: A long running site for playing Scrabble against other people or against the computer, with daily puzzles, a word finder and the official dictionary alongside the games. It is one of the few places offering real time play with the licensed board rather than an approximation of it.

items.name: mondomedia.com
items.brief: Referring IPs up 29% and subnets up 28% — one new link per network, which is the healthy shape. Rank change of 35% on an established media domain. The near-identical IP and subnet growth is what genuine link acquisition looks like and is the clearest contrast on this page with the Omsk entry.
items.description: Mondo Media, the studio and publisher behind Happy Tree Friends and Dick Figures, which has been making adult animated shorts for the web since the late 1990s. It was one of the first companies to build an audience for original animation online rather than through television, and still publishes new series on its own site.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Third day climbing and the shape got better, not worse: stars up 25% to 3,848 while forks rose 33% and open issues 58%. Forks and issues both outpacing stars means people are running the code and hitting real edges, not bookmarking it. HackerNews has gone quiet — comments up only 1.5%, off the front page — so this is now growing on its own without a thread pushing it, which is the transition most launches never make.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model on any Apple Silicon Mac in about 2 GB of memory, including the 8 GB machines, instead of loading all 14.3 GB. It keeps the shared core and the cache resident and streams only the experts each token actually needs off the SSD. The runtime, installer, command line tool and Mac app are all written in Swift and Metal, built for this one model rather than wrapping MLX or llama.cpp.

items.name: DramaWave - Dramas & Reels
items.brief: DramaWave improved its best rank 20% to position 12 while falling 34% in the US, 32% in the UK and 22% in Germany. Charting far better overall while losing every tracked Western market means the gain came from somewhere we do not watch. With 100 million Android installs already, this is a mature short-drama app moving on ad spend, not a discovery.
items.description: A streaming app for vertical short dramas, the soap opera episodes shot in portrait and cut into two minute instalments, in the same category as ReelShort and DramaBox. The format is bought heavily through social advertising, so the numbers on apps like this move with marketing spend more than with word of mouth.

items.name: FORScan Lite - for Ford, Mazda
items.brief: FORScan Lite's Android installs jumped to 10 million and reviews rose 57% in a day — an enormous move for a paid car-diagnostics tool with only 192 iOS ratings. The install figure is bucketed by Google, so a jump like that is a threshold being crossed rather than a real overnight surge. Worth watching the review count instead: 57% growth there is a genuine number.
items.description: Diagnostics software for Ford, Mazda, Lincoln and Mercury vehicles, reading the manufacturer specific fault codes and module data that a generic OBD2 scanner cannot see. It is the phone version of a tool that mechanics and owners use to configure vehicle modules rather than only to read a check engine light.

items.name: yc-software/qm
items.brief: Stars up 121% and forks up 150% in a day, with open issues up 124% and its HackerNews rank improving sharply. Forks growing faster than stars on a repo this young means people are cloning to modify rather than to watch. Everything about it is early enough that a single day could reverse it, but the fork-to-star ratio is the healthiest in today's set.
items.description: An agent harness built for a whole company rather than one person, running in Slack and on the web. Each employee gets an isolated workspace with its own memory, files, credentials and permissions, and can also work with the agent in shared channels and projects. The model and the underlying harness are swappable, so a deployment is not tied to one vendor.

items.name: sqliteai/waste
items.brief: Stars up 74% and forks up 69% while comments more than doubled to 161 against just 9 points. That comment-to-point ratio is still inverted — roughly eighteen comments per point — which means the discussion is an argument, not applause. Yesterday's question was whether the stars were the idea or the fight; two days of doubling suggests the idea is surviving the fight.
items.description: An inference engine written in C with no runtime dependencies, built to run frontier models that do not fit in memory. It holds the shared trunk of the model in RAM, streams the selected experts straight off NVMe and uses whatever memory is left as a cache. The full 2.78 trillion parameter Kimi K3, not a distilled or pruned version, runs on a 64 GB MacBook Pro at about 0.6 tokens per second.

items.name: hillelwayne.com
items.brief: 106 HackerNews comments and a small Tranco improvement. Same shape as maurycyz.com: an individual writer having a good day. The value here is the reverse of a riser — it tells you what developers are arguing about today, which is a content signal rather than a company signal.
items.description: The site of Hillel Wayne, who writes about formal methods and specification for working programmers, and who published Logic for Programmers. The posts cover TLA+, Alloy and property based reasoning, alongside long detours into software history and the origins of programming concepts.

items.name: projectpluto.com
items.brief: 79 comments on the front page with a 0.6% Tranco move. Astronomy software with a long history. The pattern across today's domain set is clear and worth naming: HackerNews plus a tiny traffic bump almost always means one popular post, not a rising business.
items.description: Project Pluto supplies astronomical software to amateur and professional astronomers, some commercial and much of it free. Find_Orb takes a set of positional measurements of an asteroid, comet or satellite and determines its orbit; Sat_ID identifies artificial satellites from an observation. These are working tools for people doing orbit determination, and several run in the browser.

items.name: seriot.ch
items.brief: HackerNews points up 20% from a base of 4, with one comment. This is noise that cleared the bar because the domain population was quiet. Listed so the set stays honest about what qualified rather than quietly dropping it.
items.description: The site of Nicolas Seriot, a software engineer who looks for computation in places nobody intended to put any. Recent work shows that three lines of Unicode transliteration rules are Turing complete on the library shipping with every major operating system, and compiles OpenStreetMap into static packs a browser rasterises without a server.

items.name: chriscoyier.net
items.brief: 52 comments, front page, 0.6% traffic gain. Chris Coyier is a well-known web developer; this is his personal site. Fourth example of the same shape today, which is a stronger argument for a gate rule about personal blogs than it is about any of these four domains.
items.description: The personal site of Chris Coyier, who founded CSS-Tricks and co-founded CodePen, and has been one of the most widely read voices in front end web development for fifteen years. The blog runs shorter and more personal than his published work, which is why a post here occasionally reaches a wider audience than the company announcement it refers to.

items.name: maurycyz.com
items.brief: HackerNews comments up 156% to 180 with its front-page rank improving 12%. A personal site pulling that much discussion is usually one essay landing rather than a site becoming popular. Worth reading what it published today; not worth tracking the domain.
items.description: A blog about electronics and software, with occasional chemistry and photography, written by someone who takes apart received wisdom and checks it. A recent piece works through the Phoebus lightbulb cartel story and shows that the usual telling gets the engineering backwards. It also keeps a hand checked list of other blogs verified as not machine generated.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Grew from 2,196 to 3,038 stars overnight — 36% — with forks up 42%, and it did that after leaving the HackerNews front page. Attention there has flattened to 1% growth while the repo itself keeps climbing, which is the split that matters: the launch is over and the growth did not stop with it. Open issues up 22% says people are running it and hitting real edges, not just bookmarking.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model on any Apple Silicon Mac in about 2 GB of memory, including the 8 GB machines, instead of loading all 14.3 GB. It keeps the shared core and the cache resident and streams only the experts each token actually needs off the SSD. The runtime, installer, command line tool and Mac app are all written in Swift and Metal, built for this one model rather than wrapping MLX or llama.cpp.

items.name: marbleos.com
items.brief: HackerNews points up 2,100% to 108 with 65 comments, front page, and nothing else in the system has seen it. This is the earliest shape RiseFinder can detect and also the least proven — one well-received post produces exactly this. Worth a look precisely because it is undecided.
items.description: MarbleOS, a desktop application that runs an AI agent as a workspace rather than a chat window, with the files, tools, tasks and outputs visible while the work happens. The pitch is the difference between something that answers you and something that goes and does the job, then hands back a document to review. It is distributed for macOS.

items.name: reclip.io
items.brief: Four points, no comments. It clears the bar only because the domain population barely moved today. Nothing to act on.
items.description: Reclip, a toolkit for video creators that finds and cuts the strongest moments out of long recordings, then generates voiceovers, removes burned in captions, compresses files and downloads source video. It packages several jobs that would normally need separate tools into one subscription, aimed at people publishing daily to TikTok, Shorts and Reels.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: The first thing this system has confirmed from three unrelated places at once — npm downloads, GitHub stars, HackerNews. Downloads are up 139% week over week against 9.9% star growth, so it is being installed far faster than it is being admired, and 64 open issues on 1,119 stars means those installs are hitting production. Watch the issue count: at this ratio the maintainer's response time decides whether it keeps the users it is winning.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: orangecrumbs.com
items.brief: Three points, no comments, same story as reclip.io. Listed for completeness; a quiet day makes small numbers rank well.
items.description: Four small tools for reading Hacker News differently, plus data stories drawn from its archive. One shows stories and comments side by side, another surfaces only the Wikipedia articles being discussed, a third collects the evergreen videos, and a fourth tracks the classic links that get resubmitted year after year. The data pieces measure things like Show HN volume rising sixfold since ChatGPT.

items.name: sqliteai/waste
items.brief: 75 comments against 9 points is an eight-to-one ratio, and that only happens when people are arguing. Stars still more than doubled and forks rose 86%, so the argument is drawing builders rather than repelling them. It is on the front page now, which means tomorrow tells you whether the stars were the idea or the fight.
items.description: An inference engine written in C with no runtime dependencies, built to run frontier models that do not fit in memory. It holds the shared trunk of the model in RAM, streams the selected experts straight off NVMe and uses whatever memory is left as a cache. The full 2.78 trillion parameter Kimi K3, not a distilled or pruned version, runs on a 64 GB MacBook Pro at about 0.6 tokens per second.

items.name: sawfwair/mere-run
items.brief: 41 stars, 14 points, 7 comments, and it has already fallen off the front page. It ranks here only because percentile scoring is relative and the population was quiet — a handful of people account for every number on this line. No conviction; listed so the set is honest about what cleared the bar.
items.description: A local first inference runtime for Apple Silicon and headless Linux, with one command line tool covering image, text, speech, vision, music, video and 3D generation, model management and an OpenAI compatible API server. The optional Mac application uses the same tool and model store rather than running a separate backend, so everything stays on the machine.

items.name: SerhiiKorniienko/bullshit-detector
items.brief: Yesterday this was up 141% on stars and 3,200% on comments; today it is up 5%. The spike is over and it converted very little — 90 stars and 4 forks from 68 comments of discussion. Comments still run level with points, so it remained an argument to the end rather than a tool anyone adopted.
items.description: A set of agent skills that fact check a YouTube video, article, tweet or PDF claim by claim, returning each claim with a verdict, a linked source and a score from zero to ten. Its rule is that no source means no verdict, even when the model is confident. The published example takes 60 claims from a video with 2.7 million views and searches 44 of them individually.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Forks up 20% and open issues up 40% against 11.9% star growth — the third day running that usage has outpaced attention on this one. Six open issues on 567 stars is still a clean tracker, so the friction is early rather than accumulating. The HackerNews points reading dropped to zero while 87 comments remain, which is more likely a flagged post than a collapse in interest.
items.description: A single native binary that runs the complete 2.8 trillion parameter Kimi K3 on consumer hardware with nothing pruned and nothing skipped. Small draft models are allowed to guess ahead for speed, but K3 checks every guess, so quality is never traded away. The published benchmark history shows throughput on an M1 Max laptop rising from 0.014 to 0.29 tokens per second over three weeks.

items.name: DramaWave - Dramas & Reels
items.brief: DramaWave improved its best rank 5% while losing ground in Germany, the UK and the US at once — 16% in the US alone. That combination only works if it is charting hard in a market outside the four tracked here. Same short-drama category as DramaBox and the same read: watch the category, not the app.
items.description: A streaming app for vertical short dramas, the soap opera episodes shot in portrait and cut into two minute instalments, in the same category as ReelShort and DramaBox. The format is bought heavily through social advertising, so the numbers on apps like this move with marketing spend more than with word of mouth.

items.name: Reelo - Media Hub
items.brief: Reelo holds rank 7 on a paid chart with 10 ratings and 5,000 Android installs. Those numbers do not belong together: a paid chart position that high on that little evidence usually means a thin category rather than a real hit. It slipped in both the UK and US today. Treat as a category artefact until a second source says otherwise.
items.description: A client for watching your own media library on Apple devices, connecting to a home media server rather than a streaming service. Apps in this category live or die on how well they handle formats the device cannot play natively, and on whether they work offline.

items.name: Claude by Anthropic
items.brief: Claude reversed yesterday's slide, gaining 7.6% in Japan and about 1.5% in both the UK and US while holding second place overall. Yesterday it was losing ground in exactly the markets it gained in today, which usually means a short campaign or a news cycle rather than anything structural. Two days does not make a trend, but the direction flipped cleanly.
items.description: Anthropic's Claude application for iPhone and iPad. As an entity here it is useful mainly as a control: a major model provider's consumer app is not an unknown rising, so movement on it measures how the App Store charts respond to a release rather than anything about early adoption.

items.name: LukeTandjung/base-gpui
items.brief: Comments up 66.7% against 4.7% star growth, on a 45-star repo. Everything about this is small enough that a handful of people account for all of it. It scores highly only because percentile ranking is relative — in a quiet population, modest movement ranks well. Worth one more day before treating it as anything.
items.description: A port of Base UI's headless component library to GPUI, the interface framework Zed is built on. It brings across compound parts, controlled and uncontrolled state, keyboard interaction and accessibility semantics, and leaves every component unstyled so applications keep full control of appearance. The implementation is written for GPUI's immediate mode rendering rather than translated from React internals.

items.name: drumih/turbo-fieldfare
items.brief: Forks grew 41.5% in a day against 18.6% star growth — people are copying it to build on roughly twice as fast as they are bookmarking it, which is the healthier of the two ratios. At 2,196 stars with 326 HackerNews comments it is past the point where a single post explains the numbers. It has already left the front page, so the next two days separate a launch spike from a tool that stuck.
items.description: Runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model on any Apple Silicon Mac in about 2 GB of memory, including the 8 GB machines, instead of loading all 14.3 GB. It keeps the shared core and the cache resident and streams only the experts each token actually needs off the SSD. The runtime, installer, command line tool and Mac app are all written in Swift and Metal, built for this one model rather than wrapping MLX or llama.cpp.

items.name: reflex-dev/xy
items.brief: Forks up 17.9% and open issues up 25.5% against only 8.5% star growth. The same shape as deltafin: usage outpacing attention. At 1,007 stars with 59 open issues this is a project being deployed rather than starred, and the 46 HackerNews comments suggest the discussion is technical rather than promotional.
items.description: A charting library for Python, from the team behind the Reflex web framework. It renders interactive charts directly from Python objects, so the analysis and the chart live in the same place instead of the data being handed to a JavaScript layer to draw. It ships on PyPI, and that is what makes the adoption measurable: a download is someone installing it into a project, a star is someone bookmarking it, and those two numbers have been moving in opposite directions here for two weeks.

items.name: openai/codex-security
items.brief: Still climbing three days after first appearing: stars up 18.8% and forks up 18.3% in the last twenty-four hours, now at 7,237 and 472. It remains on the HackerNews front page with 197 comments. Sustained growth at this size is the strongest pattern in today's set — most launches decay by day three, and this one has not.
items.description: A command line tool and TypeScript SDK from OpenAI that scans a codebase for security vulnerabilities, validates what it finds and proposes fixes. It runs against OpenAI's models by default but takes any provider, and a deep scan mode can run for hours across many workers. Some categories of finding require approved access before the tool will return them.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Open issues jumped 300% while forks rose 26.8% and stars 15.2%. Issue counts growing faster than stars means people are running it and hitting problems, not admiring the README. That friction is a better adoption signal than a clean tracker, though it also means the project is about to be tested by how fast the maintainer responds.
items.description: A single native binary that runs the complete 2.8 trillion parameter Kimi K3 on consumer hardware with nothing pruned and nothing skipped. Small draft models are allowed to guess ahead for speed, but K3 checks every guess, so quality is never traded away. The published benchmark history shows throughput on an M1 Max laptop rising from 0.014 to 0.29 tokens per second over three weeks.

items.name: experientiallabs/world-model-optimizer
items.brief: On the HackerNews front page with points up 40.9% and comments up 22.7% in a day. Stars grew 18.6% but the watcher count sits at 1 against 255 stars — almost nobody has committed to following it. That gap is the thing to watch: front-page attention with no followers usually evaporates within the week.
items.description: Takes the traces an AI agent produces in production and turns them into a cheaper agent. It builds a simulation from those traces, fits a router that decides which model each request should go to, then trains a small open model for the specific workload. The point is to stop paying frontier prices for every request when most of them do not need it.

items.name: mishushakov/desktui
items.brief: Appears in today's corroborated set on both GitHub and HackerNews. Early-stage terminal UI work, and like base-gpui the absolute numbers are small enough that the percentages overstate the case. Listed for completeness rather than conviction.
items.description: A VNC client that draws a remote desktop inside a terminal window as actual pixels, using the Kitty graphics protocol rather than approximating the screen with coloured half blocks. It handles clipboard in both directions in UTF-8, a view only mode, live rescaling and quality settings for slow links. The author built it over a weekend to test what current coding models could do.

items.name: FrigadeHQ/yap
items.brief: Modest and clean — stars up 8% to 290, forks up 16%, 104 HackerNews points with 43 comments. Nothing here is dramatic, which is why it is worth noting: the numbers are in proportion to each other rather than one spiking alone.
items.description: Voice dictation for macOS that runs on the device using Apple's own speech framework, with no account, no API key and no audio leaving the machine. Press a shortcut, talk, press it again, and the text lands in whatever field you were already typing in. Transcripts are kept locally so anything can be copied again later. It is free and open source.

items.name: SerhiiKorniienko/bullshit-detector
items.brief: Comments jumped 3,200% to 66 and points 178% to 62 — a one-to-one comment-to-point ratio, which almost always means argument rather than approval. Open issues rose 800% from a tiny base while stars grew 28%. It has already fallen off the front page, so the next two days decide whether the attention converts into anything.
items.description: A set of agent skills that fact check a YouTube video, article, tweet or PDF claim by claim, returning each claim with a verdict, a linked source and a score from zero to ten. Its rule is that no source means no verdict, even when the model is confident. The published example takes 60 claims from a video with 2.7 million views and searches 44 of them individually.

items.name: wassgha/rescript
items.brief: Forks up 11% and open issues up 40% against 16% star growth, with 43 forks on 384 stars. That ratio is unusually high — better than one fork per nine stars — and suggests a tool people modify for their own use rather than adopt as-is.
items.description: A video and audio editor where you edit the transcript instead of a timeline. Drop in a file and it is transcribed on the device with per word timestamps and speaker labels; delete a word and the matching piece of media is cut. Nothing is uploaded, and it runs either in a browser or as a desktop application on macOS, Windows and Linux.

items.name: openai/codex-security
items.brief: Forks up 70% and open issues up 84% against 47% star growth, reaching 6,090 stars and 399 forks. Issues climbing faster than stars is the signature of a repository people are running rather than reading, and at this size that means real deployments hitting real edges. On the HackerNews front page with 197 comments, which explains the arrival but not the fork ratio — that part is adoption.
items.description: A command line tool and TypeScript SDK from OpenAI that scans a codebase for security vulnerabilities, validates what it finds and proposes fixes. It runs against OpenAI's models by default but takes any provider, and a deep scan mode can run for hours across many workers. Some categories of finding require approved access before the tool will return them.

items.name: gavamedia/deltafin
items.brief: Forks up 63% against 42% star growth, on the HackerNews front page with 87 comments. A fork-to-star ratio that high on a 429-star project means people are cloning to modify, not to bookmark. Open issues sitting at 1 says nobody has hit a wall yet, which is either a clean codebase or too early to tell.
items.description: A single native binary that runs the complete 2.8 trillion parameter Kimi K3 on consumer hardware with nothing pruned and nothing skipped. Small draft models are allowed to guess ahead for speed, but K3 checks every guess, so quality is never traded away. The published benchmark history shows throughput on an M1 Max laptop rising from 0.014 to 0.29 tokens per second over three weeks.

items.name: twalichiewicz/HNewhere
items.brief: 419 HackerNews points with comments up 22%, but only 192 stars and 7 forks. Attention running far ahead of adoption: a lot of people found it interesting and very few took it home. It has left the front page, so this is close to its peak unless the star count starts closing the gap.
items.description: A small userscript that shows the Hacker News discussion for whatever page you are reading, if that page has ever been submitted. It closes the gap between finding an article and finding out what people said about it, which normally means a separate search on a separate site.

items.name: Parchment: Agenda & Daily Note
items.brief: Parchment improved its best paid-chart rank 12% while falling in all three tracked paid markets, on just 124 ratings and a million Android installs. The rating count is far too small for the install figure, which usually means the Android and iOS audiences are very different sizes — worth checking before treating either number as the whole picture.
items.description: A private daily journal for iPhone that keeps writing, plans, calendar entries and reminders in one place rather than splitting them across four apps. The category is crowded, so what matters for an app like this is whether the calendar integration is good enough to replace the separate planner people already use.

items.name: Claude by Anthropic
items.brief: Claude held the number one position across its tracked storefronts, gaining 3.6% in the UK while slipping slightly in Japan and the US. At 50 million Android installs and 215,000 ratings this is a competitive read rather than a discovery — the value is in which market moves which way, week to week.
items.description: Anthropic's Claude application for iPhone and iPad. As an entity here it is useful mainly as a control: a major model provider's consumer app is not an unknown rising, so movement on it measures how the App Store charts respond to a release rather than anything about early adoption.
